chapter-two.title: Chapter Two: Many Roots, No Single Beginning

begin-with-uncertainty.title: A Good Origin Story Is Not Always a True One
begin-with-uncertainty.body:
I wanted Chhau to have one clear beginning. A founder, a date, a court, a battlefield, or a village would have made the chapter easier to write.

The evidence does not give us that.

Historical accounts point instead to several overlapping layers: martial exercise, seasonal ritual, agrarian and community life, princely patronage, regional storytelling, and later movement onto institutional and international stages. Different writers give each layer a different importance. [2][3][5][9]

The three traditions also need separate histories. Evidence from Mayurbhanj cannot automatically explain Purulia. A story preserved by Seraikella’s royal household cannot stand in for every village troupe. Shared features suggest contact, but they do not prove one single event of origin.

Some course materials gather useful names and theories but do not provide bibliographies. They are leads, not final answers. [16][17][19][21]

This chapter therefore begins with a sentence I originally did not want to write: **we do not know one single beginning for all Chhau.**

That uncertainty is not a failure. It is the most honest starting point.

martial-inheritance.title: When Combat Becomes Performance
martial-inheritance.body:
Many accounts connect Chhau with regional systems of exercise and combat training, including sword-and-shield practice and paika or akhara traditions. Wide stances, quick changes of direction, mock attack and defence, jumps, and weapon phrases make that relationship visible. Mayurbhanj histories give it particular importance. [2][3][4][5]

But resemblance is not the whole origin story.

A movement changes when it enters performance. A strike becomes a line the audience can read. A defensive position becomes a pause. A leap can identify a hero, demon, hunter, or animal. Rhythm reorganises the action, costume changes its size, and the audience reads an image where a fighter once read danger.

The akhara is important here. It is a training ground, but it is also a community of teachers, students, musicians, and senior practitioners. Knowledge passes through demonstration, correction, repetition, and shared time—not through a paragraph alone. [2][4][6]

> Watch: A responsible video for this page should show a practitioner explaining how one combat-derived action changes when it becomes theatrical. It should not present a generic sword pose as historical proof or safe practice.

The martial inheritance helps explain discipline, readiness, endurance, and spatial awareness. It does not explain every mask, melody, ritual, story, or regional difference.

festival-ritual-community.title: The Dance Has a Season and a Crowd
festival-ritual-community.body:
Chhau did not grow only inside a rehearsal room or a modern theatre.

Its histories belong to festival seasons, public gatherings, training grounds, makers’ workshops, musicians, organisers, families, and audiences.

The month of Chaitra, around March and April, is especially important. Chaitra Parva is closely connected with Chhau performance in Mayurbhanj and Seraikella. Purulia Chhau belongs to a wider local festival life that includes Chaitra and Gajan observances in some places, as well as other community occasions. The exact calendar and ritual setting differ by region and locality. [1][2][3][8][10]

A festival can organise months of preparation. Dancers rehearse. Musicians refine cues. Costumes and masks are repaired or made. Junior members watch senior members. An audience learns to recognise characters, rhythms, and entrances over years.

This context explains choices that may look excessive on a small indoor screen. A broad gesture travels across an open ground. Strong drumming gathers attention through noise. A bright or enlarged mask remains visible at night and from a distance.

> Listen: The audio needed here is not a clean instrument sample alone. It should include the sound of an open performance ground—the call, the crowd, the entrance, and the way rhythm establishes the space.

court-village-stage.title: Who Supported Chhau—and Who Did the Work?
court-village-stage.body:
Chhau is sometimes divided into two “court styles” and one “village style.” The phrase points to real histories, but it can hide more than it explains.

The former princely houses of Mayurbhanj and Seraikella played important roles in supporting, organising, and reshaping their regional traditions. Patronage could provide rehearsal structures, musicians, festival support, choreographic attention, and opportunities to travel. Members of Seraikella’s ruling family are closely linked with repertoire, while the Bhanj court is important in Mayurbhanj’s history. [3][5][9]

Patronage is not the same as invention.

Courts depended on dancers, gurus, musicians, makers, and communities whose labour made performance possible. Archives often preserve powerful names more clearly than the names of working artists.

Purulia’s history is more often told through village troupes, community festivals, local organisers, and mask-making networks. It also includes local royal support, public institutions, tourism, state programmes, awards, researchers, and national and international stages. [8][9]

During the twentieth century, all three traditions entered new theatres, institutions, cities, festivals, recordings, and touring programmes. Wider visibility created opportunities, but also pressure to shorten, simplify, or reward spectacle over subtlety.

The useful question is not “court or village?” It is: **who supported the work, who carried the knowledge, and who is remembered by name?**

meaning-of-chhau.title: What Does the Word “Chhau” Mean?
meaning-of-chhau.body:
There is no single proven answer.

Writers and practitioners connect the word _Chhau_ with several possibilities. One links it with _chhaya_, meaning shadow, image, or shade. Another links it with _chhauni_, a camp or military encampment. _Chadma_ means disguise. Other explanations refer to attack, concealment, hunting cries, or regional words whose spellings vary between sources. [5][7][9][16]

Each theory seems to notice something real: masks, martial memory, image, disguise, or action.

But a theory that fits one tradition may fit another less comfortably. Mayurbhanj is unmasked, so an explanation based only on masks cannot fully explain the shared name as the traditions exist today. A military explanation helps us read part of the movement history, but it does not explain ritual, music, or later choreography.

Similar sound is not proof of linguistic origin.

So the glossary in this book gives a simple definition: **Chhau is the collective name for the Mayurbhanj, Seraikella, and Purulia dance traditions of eastern India.**

The argument about where the word came from remains open.
